speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER UNDER INQUIRIES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table order in council P.C. 1954-760 appointing as a commissioner under the Inquiries Act the Hon. W. F. A. Turgeon, Q.C., LL.D., a member of the Queen's privy council for Canada, to inquire into the application and effects of agreed charges made by the railways under part 4 of the Transport Act.
Hon. members will recall that in 1951 the Railway Act was amended to provide that where competitive transcontinental tariffs are established by the railways, freight rates on the same goods shipped to or from intermediate points shall not exceed by more than one-third the rates in such competitive transcontinental tariffs. This amendment was made in accordance with one of the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation, of which the Hon. Mr. Turgeon was chairman.
The government of the province of Alberta has recently made representations to this government that this so-called one and one-third rule in the Railway Act should be extended by parliament to apply to agreed charges made by the railways with the authorization of the board of transport commissioners under part I, section 4 of the Transport Act. The government has come to the conclusion that this proposal requires detailed study before its merits can be properly assessed. There are many interests involved -those of producers, purchasers, the railways and other transportation agencies and the public generally at intermediate points as well as in eastern Canada and on the Pacific coast. The subject is one which is closely related to the subject matter of the report of the royal commission on transportation but on which the commission did not make any recommendation. Consequently the government has arranged with the Hon. Mr. Turgeon to serve as a commissioner to inquire into this particular question of agreed charges, taking into account the representations that
have been made on it and all other relevant considerations including developments since the royal commission reported in 1951.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take just one minute to refer to the report of the debate which took place on the bill yesterday which appears in the Montreal Gazette this morning under the heading "Military Inventions Unprotected". I have not the slightest doubt that this Canadian Press report was written in perfect good faith but in the first paragraph it says the precise opposite of what I said in the house, and I do not think that is an impression that any hon. member would want to have spread about. It said:
State Secretary Pickersgill said today there is no law to prevent a privately-owned invention of a1 military nature from becoming public property and reaching a potential enemy.
[DOT]5054

Inventions by Public Servants What I actually said in reply to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) who made a most useful intervention on this point yesterday was that the law did provide, in so far as we thought the law could do so, for precisely this kind of thing in sections 20, 21 and 22 of the Patent Act and that under the provisions of the law it was the duty of the commissioner to see that such applications are scrutinized in the kind of way that the Leader of the Opposition had in mind before anything is made public about them. The government has been given authority to keep them secret if they have military significance.
I felt it only right yesterday to go on and point out that there was one danger against which the law could not, as far as we could see, provide, namely that if someone invented something and, for example, did not try to patent it but rather made a speech about it or wrote an article about it or something of that sort, no law could prevent that kind of thing. In view of what was said yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition I feel that it would be desirable, when the commission of inquiry into the Patent Act is set up, to have this point drawn particularly to the attention of that inquiry and I shall be glad to do so.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the [DOT]Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR OWNERSHIP, MANAGEMENT AND PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) has raised this point,
I should like to supplement the remarks he has made because I appreciate greatly the manner in which this subject is being approached. My concern related to a warning Which had been given by Sir Robert Watson-Watt with regard to the possibility of very important secrets being disclosed in the filing of patents. I welcome the statement by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) that when the patent commission is being set up he will draw to their attention the necessity of guarding in some way against the dangers pointed out by Sir Robert Watson-Watt as exemplified by the disclosure of the Whittle patent to German agents resulting in the actual development of the jet engine in Germany before it was developed in Britain. I welcome this assurance, but in view of the assurance may I also add the suggestion that Sir Robert Watson-Watt made, namely that in addition to being as careful as possible to prevent the filing of patents which would disclose very important secrets care should also be taken that anything of that kind should not become a barrier to development, and the lack of enthusiasm for a new idea on the part of officials should not be permitted to become in itself a hindrance to development.


I recognize that this presents a very great problem for the consideration of the commission. I would refer to the speech of Sir Robert Watson-Watt in which he suggested a combination of technical and official skill in order to determine the very difficult balance between protection against publicity on the one side and on the other side protection against interference with possible development.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there has been considerable discussion of the bill now before us. We have had an explanation from the minister and the bill has been discussed in the standing committee. I think it is possible to say that in the way this problem is being attacked it is being attacked by men with little confidence in the future of at least part of the area which the line in the province of Quebec is designed to serve. Those who have little thoughts are going to accomplish only little things. Those who have great thoughts and great confidence are going to accomplish great things. I think that those of us who have true faith-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
-not only in the central area of Canada, not only in the parts which are already built up, not only in the parts which have already proved themselves, but who also have faith in the hinterlands of this country, in the areas about which we do not know a great deal yet except that we do know they hold great promise, are disturbed, worried and unhappy about the attitude displayed in the information given us on this bill.
I think we can call it a sort of lick and promise bill. One half of it is the lick inasmuch as we are informed that half the line will be built, and the other half is the promise because we have no indication as to when, how or under what circumstances the second section of the line will be built. It is a lick and a promise measure, one part of the line to be built in the immediate future and with respect to the other part a rather vague and indefinite promise extending far into the future. One of the things we must note about the bill is that it contains the indication that any time within the next ten years the second section of the line may be constructed, and if it is not convenient to do so within the next ten years then at any time in the future beyond the ten year period, beyond the year 1964 mentioned in the bill, the governor in council may continue its provisions in force in order that the line may then be constructed.
Can anything, Mr. Chairman, be much more indefinite than that? Can anything be much more foolish in the light of the circumstances than to suggest that we should build a railway line, half of which we will build now leaving the end almost suspended in mid-air, and the other half, the half which logically completes the line, the half which runs to the sea, the half which connects finally with a seaport which can become great, will not be built until some indefinite time in the future? The minister and the witnesses who appeared before the standing committee advanced reasons why this course is being followed. From the information given to us I think these reasons may be summarized by saying that the part of the line extending from Beattyville to Chibougamau is to be built through an area from which sufficient traffic can be guaranteed for the railroad line through signed contracts to ensure beyond any shadow of doubt that it will be an economically feasible proposition. The other half is to be built through territory where, according to the information given to us, such written guarantees are not possible.
Canadian National Railways
In the light of that the minister suggests: Let us build the line in so far, so to speak, as the money is on the line, but let us not take any chance, let us not have any faith, let us not go beyond that point and develop the rest of the line. Let us simply leave that hanging in the air as a promise. When we examine the minister's statement we find that he says that he will build it at some time in the future. He and the witnesses who appeared before the committee indicated that they know there is promise in that area, that some day they will be able to build the line, and that almost from the day their trains run over it they will have an indication that it will be a profitable part of their operations. We then ask: What indications are there that this change is going to take place? What is going to happen between Chibougamau and St. Felicien in the next few years that will make this economic change possible? We know of nothing, we cannot pinpoint anything, that is going to happen. We just believe that the natural growth of the country is going to merit the construction of this line within the next few years. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, thereon hangs one of the most disturbing facets of this entire proposition. There is no concrete indication that anything is going to happen in that particular territory within the next few years to merit the building of this line.
We are told by the minister that he definitely plans to build it within the next few years. To me, Mr. Chairman, that indicates clearly a lack of confidence that this line is going to be actually built. If these things are going to happen-I believe they will happen, I know they will happen because they have happened so often before in this country-within the next four or five years, they could be speeded up immeasurably, the area could be made more profitable and more interesting, more developmental projects could be undertaken immediately upon the construction of this line. But if we are going to stand back and wait for the normal growth of the territory, we are displaying a lack of confidence, and worse than that we are putting off until some indefinite date in the future the construction of a line that merits building now.
It seems to me, and I think to many others, that we have a choice here between helping the growth of this area through the building of the railways and waiting for the growth of the area to help the building of the railway, the two propositions being unalterably opposed to one another. The development of Canada, almost without exception, has followed not preceded the construction of our

Canadian National Railways great railroads. The west was opened up following upon the construction of the great railway line which this party supported. The other part, the area around Hudson bay, for example, and mining and lumbering particularly, developed as a result of the growth of that railroad that is now known as the Ontario Northland railroad, or the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railroad, as I like to think of it.
We cannot expect people to go into an area, to open up mines, to construct mills, to cut lumber and to do all these things to aid industrial growth, if we, as a government and as a nation, do not have sufficient confidence in the area ourselves to supply them with the basic transportation that it is essential for them to have. Let us remember that if this line is built in its entirety it will have at one end Chicoutimi and Port Alfred. Port Alfred is a deep-water port at the head of the Saguenay river, a port which even now handles a great volume of shipping. Almost all of this shipping is concerned with the area immediately around Chicoutimi and Port Alfred. If the railroad line were built it would run back from there over an area that is rich in timberland, that has great agricultural possibilities, an area of which we do not yet know the mineral possibilities. It will go into Chibougamau, where some of Canada's greatest mines are located, and then over the line that it is already agreed to build immediately and cut back over another area of great mineralization. Ultimately, it will go through Beattyville and into Noranda, thus connecting up the great territory of Ontario and Quebec, which would become tributary to Port Alfred and Chicoutimi. Through the port would then flow, over far less rail miles than are now necessary, supplies for a great part of Canada which must now get them at greater expense through more southerly ports.
Let us remember, Mr. Chairman, that if this government does not have confidence in that area at least the provincial government has, and has backed that confidence by the construction of a road from Chicoutimi into that territory. Approximately $4 million went into the building of the road. At the end of it grew mines where there were no mines before; there grew industry where there was no industry; there grew merchandising and marketing as well as a city, where there was no city before. These things are the result of confidence, the result of a belief in the future and the result of doing something. I am not standing here, Mr. Chairman, to make a political argument out of this thing. I am standing here because I come


from a province which, in the past few years, has grown into something that one would hardly have believed possible.
As I argue for the construction of this railroad line, I am thinking of the man, for example, who threw away his hammer near Cobalt and dislodged a piece of ore that resulted in the building of mines, cities and industries that one would not have believed existed. I am thinking of the fact, that always in the development of this country we have developed one area and said there is nothing beyond that. We did not believe very much lay beyond that. Then, our pioneers have gone forth, our people who would just not take that sort of reasoning, and risked their lives, if they were that kind of men; they have risked their capital if they were that kind of entrepreneur; and they have brought us the things that have made this nation great. They have brought us tremendous areas that are now devoted to agriculture. They have brought us the great watersheds, the great sources of pulp-wood which now floats down to our paper mills.
All these things, Mr. Chairman, have been the result of not sitting on our posteriors and saying that there is no certainty that this proposition is going to pay from the date it is built. They have been the result, rather, of faith, and with that faith came the results which we wanted. The great fortunes, and there have been great fortunes, that have been built in this country have not been the result of wanting something certain. They have been the result of taking a chance, a measured chance based on the confidence that it would turn out the way it should and the way that would be best for the country as a whole.
And so, to sum up, lest someone say subsequently that this is visionary, that this is impossible, that this is asking the government to assume, through the construction of a portion of this railroad line from Chibougamau to St. Felicien, a burden which will continue into the indefinite future, let us recapitulate. We are suggesting that while the idea behind the bill we are now considering in committee is an excellent one, of which we wholly approve, the bill falls short in so far as it builds only one-half of the line which, only in its entirety, can do what it is supposed to do. The half of the line which it is not proposed to build immediately is the half which would connect a great area with a seaport, the half which would traverse an area which is rich in resources, the half which would connect an area of mines, which need smelters, with a community which is

now considering the erection of one smelter, and is planning the erection of another in the field of zinc.
The half of this line, Mr. Chairman, which is not being built is the half which confidence in our country and faith in its future dictates should be built. And, Mr. Chairman, to the extent that people do not build this line, and do not support its building now, immediately, they display to all the world a lack of confidence and a lack of faith for the future of one of the greatest areas in Canada.

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think I am as capable as the hon. member who has just taken his seat of adding any new material to the discussion. I think he has done very well; but I would point out that this bill has been Considered by one of the best committees of the House of Commons, where we have had before us officials who have given us much information. The minister convinced us that he has been assured it would pay; and all we have to do is to read the reports.
I do not want to attempt to shut off debate, but I believe the road is needed and that the bill meets that need. The minister has convinced us that it will pay.

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
Before the clause carries I should like to say a word. Hon. members will have noticed that in it there is provision to give to the governor in council authority to build such portion of the lines as the governor in council may decide is necessary, prior to December 31, 1964, or such later date as the governor in council may fix.
I think all hon. members will agree that the building of railways is a matter of concern to the people of Canada, including members of parliament. Officials of the railways gave the committee an explanation as to why one part of the railway should be built immediately, but pointed out that the revenue in sight would not warrant the building of the other part mentioned in the bill. I think most hon. members will agree that a quite reasonable argument was presented on the point.
That being so I do not see why the government should ask parliament now to give it a blank cheque to build this other part of the railway any time within the next ten years, prior to December 31, 1964 or, if it is not built by that time, by such later date as the governor in council may fix. I suggest that is a very dangerous principle, and I am sure if the government did not have such
Canadian National Railways a large majority in parliament this kind of legislation would not be presented to us. Therefore I move, in amendment:
That clause 1 be amended by deleting therefrom the words, "or such later date as the governor in council may fix".
As I said before, parliament has always been most anxious to give its support to the building of any railway line that would be feasible; and I should think that ten years would give the cabinet plenty of opportunity to build this extra line. If however by 1963 work on this branch line was started but would not be completed before December 31, 1964, I am sure parliament at that date would be most co-operative in extending the period. But I think it is undemocratic for this parliament to tie the hands of all parliaments in the future to a proposition which is not more definite than the one now before us.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must confess I have not yet heard any satisfactory explanation as to why the date should be set so far ahead. I am not speaking alone of the amendment suggesting the removal of these words from the clause. I do not know that the amendment will satisfy the situation because, if it were going to be much later than 1964, I am not sure that this parliament would be particularly interested in the matter.
This line could be completed in a comparatively short time; and I must confess I am wholly at a loss to understand the government's position in deferring the date until 1964 if, in fact, it has any intention to proceed. Now that the amendment is before us I should like to hear from the minister, not merely as to why there should be a later date mentioned, but why a date as late as 1964 should be used.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
I am glad the Leader of the Opposition has suggested that I make an explanation. I would point out that the explanation has already been made in committee, because the argument now offered by the hon. member who has moved the amendment was made before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I do not know that he moved an amendment in committee, but certainly he made the point forcibly more than once.
To explain the position I believe I could put it thus: As the matter now stands, the Canadian National Railways have obtained guarantees from a number of corporations and companies, which would confirm the financial estimate of the railway in so far as that part of the line is concerned which extends from Beattyville on the west to Chi-bougamau in about the centre of the arc from Beattyville to St. Felicien. But, in so far as

Canadian National Railways the other half of the line is concerned, namely that part extending from St. Felicien to Chibougamau, the Canadian National Railways, through their officers, have given evidence to the effect that, from a financial standpoint, the position is such that they would not recommend the immediate construction of that portion at this time.
However, they are hopeful that with the construction of the line from Beattyville to Chibougamau industry will be encouraged, and that it will, in fact, see the establishment of a zinc refinery, or even of a copper refinery, in the lake St. John area, perhaps at Chicoutimi itself, in which case it would then be profitable, if the Canadian National Railways obtained the necessary guarantees, to continue the construction of the line on to St. Felicien. So that it may be possible to begin the construction of the east end of the line fairly soon. It may not be possible to begin it within the ten years and that is why the government have seen fit to accept that recommendation of the railways. After all, the Canadian National Railways is the body responsible for the construction of the lines that have been built from time to time with the approval of parliament.
It may not be possible to complete the line within ten years. If that should be so, then it was felt that this authority would enable Canadian National Railways to construct the line even after the ten years, and for that reason the clause is worded as it is.

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext: May I just say one word. Since this parliament is responsible when the Canadian National Railways have deficits, we should be called upon to decide, after hearing representations of the railway, whether this extension is economic at the time it is proposed to make it. My hon. friend is on very sound ground in asking the committee to delete the authority of the governor general in council. From time to time we have argued against governor-in-council decisions. This is the kind of decision which under no circumstances should be approved of. If the time comes when the railway can show that this extension is economic, then the railway can come to the house and ask for the authority to make the extension at that time. We should delete this very objectionable feature of the bill at this time.

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the ordinary enabling legislation of this kind, under which the Canadian National Railways is authorized to construct a branch line, the first section sets out that the governor in council may provide for the railway to build the line from one point to another point within a

certain set period of time, which is a reasonable time for completion. That was the practice followed in the case of the branch line from Terrace to Kitimat, British Columbia, and from Sherridon to Lynn Lake in Manitoba, and I believe also in the case of the line from Barraute to Kiask Falls in Quebec; but here we have two very significant variations.
In the first place, we find the words: "in whole or in part" qualifying the completion, so that the governor in council may authorize only the completion of a part of this railway. As I pointed out, in all the other bills the authorization must cover the completion of the whole line. I repeat, here we have these very significant words, "in whole or in part".
Then instead of having a time set within which the railway could reasonably be constructed, we have a time limit of ten years, to December 31, 1964. There again is a provision completely different from the standard provision written into legislation of this kind.
The amendment of the hon. member for Mackenzie is a sound one, because, while these qualifications "or such later date as the governor in council may fix" are used in the other enabling laws to which I have referred, it was done because there might be some slip in completing by the date set, and therefore the precaution was taken of allowing what I am sure was intended to be a slight extension. But here the effect of the extension is to add it on to the ten-year period.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext: From here to eternity.

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
Yes, from here to eternity. In the first place, that line need be built only in whole or in part, and then it need not be finished until 1964, and then the governor in council may put it off after that time just as long as he sees fit, which may mean that the line will not be constructed for fifteen or twenty years.
The position we have taken is that the government came into the house and asked authority to build the line from Beattyville to St. Felicien. Well, why not go ahead and build it instead of having this qualification of building half now and the other half in five years, ten years, fifteen years or twenty years.
The vice-president of the Canadian National Railways in charge of development indicated before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines that the eastern half of the line would be a development project; in other words, that there was not the traffic there to make the line pay immediately. He advocated it on the basis of its being a development project.

He went on to say the C.N.R. hoped that there would be established at Chicoutimi a great zinc smelter which would handle zinc concentrates from the whole of Quebec and Ontario. This bill covers also a short line in Ontario called the lake Manitouwadge line, and in the lake Manitouwadge area there is zinc ore. The vice-president said it was hoped that zinc ore from as far as the lake Manitouwadge area, which is up near Port Arthur in Ontario, would be taken by the C.N.R. right across to Chicoutimi, and in Chicoutimi there would be a smelter.
There are also of course great power resources in the Chicoutimi area. There is the foundation for a great development in Canada. But at the same time the government takes the position that this connecting line from Chibougamau to St. Felicien need not be built for at least ten years and perhaps longer. How they expect to get a zinc smelter at Chicoutimi with that gap in the line of 139 or 140 miles from Chibougamau to St. Felicien, I cannot quite see. They are expecting private industry to go into Chicoutimi and build a $25 million smelter without the railway being connected. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that that does not make sense at all.
Either this is actually a development project or it is not, and if it is a development project which is in the interests of the nation -and the minister said on second reading that it was in the interests of the nation- then the government should go ahead and build the whole railway. Certainly the amendment moved by the hon. member for Mackenzie is a proper one and I would hope that it would be carried by the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
May I refer to the question raised by the leader of the C.C.F. party. I view his query in this fashion. As he knows, in respect of the previous branch lines which were built a statement is tabled in the house within a certain number of days after the house meets. That was the case with the Lynn Lake line and with the Barraute-Kiask line. These reports form part of the subject matter which is dealt with by the officers of the Canadian National Railways in the committee on railways and shipping, and each year it is therefore possible for the members of that committee or any other member to find out what the position of the line is.
The reason why the words, "1964 or such later date as the governor in council may fix", are in there is that we were following practically word for word previous legislation. If my hon. friend looks up section 1 of chapter 20, 1 Elizabeth II, an act respecting construction of lines of railways by the
Canadian National Railways Canadian National Railway Company from Terrace to Kitimat, he will see the same wording, namely:
The governor in council may provide for the construction and completion by Canadian National Railway Company prior to the first day of November. nineteen hundred and fifty-four, or such later date as the governor in council may fix.
Likewise, in 1951, 15 George VI, chapter 44, an act respecting the construction of a line by the Canadian National Railway Company from Sherridon to Lynn Lake, there is a similar provision, namely:
The governor in council may provide for the construction and completion by Canadian National Railway Company . . . prior to the first day of November, nineteen hundred and fifty-three, or such later date as the governor in council may fix . . .
Therefore, the wording in both cases is exactly the same. It is not sought here to take the extraordinary powers such as have been suggested. On the contrary, the legislation has been based on the experience of two, if not three, similar lines, and the only reason, which I do not wish to repeat again, other than that which I have already advanced, is what I said in answer to the Leader of the Opposition a moment ago. It would strike me that for that reason we should not accept the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Mackenzie.

I think it is unfortunate that the legislation is before parliament in this particular form. Parliament, I believe, is quite prepared to give support to the spending of $17 million for the construction of the Beattyville branch, but if we pass this bill the railway will be able at any time in the future to proceed with the spending of $17 million for the construction of the remaining 139-mile branch, and I believe that is unfair to parliament.

Unfortunately, political pressure at election time has been responsible for the building in Canada of branch lines which have been a headache for succeeding governments, and I think no government should ask parliament to vote $17 million for the construction of a branch line by order in council at some time in the future. The people of the Saguenay district are determined to work constructively and intelligently for the fulfilment of the project. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I am confident that as a result of the guarantees we will give or of the subsidies that may be granted by the government, we shall be in a position to undertake the building of the eastern section of the railroad within a year at the most.

Mr. Chairman, I think this piece of legislation is very peculiarly drafted because what we have before us is, in effect, two different bills. There is one bill which the government has a real intention of going through with. This bill is to build a railway line from Beattyville to Chibougamau. The government should have another bill for the building of a railway from Chibougamau to St. Felicien and should explain to us the various reasons and so forth. The minister might say that I am making a political speech, but it is quite evident that in drafting the present bill in its present form the government was just trying to appease public opinion in the lake St. John region and that that was about all. The government did not have the immediate intention of building the eastern part of this railway. The government had the immediate intention of building a railroad from Beattyville to Chibougamau and it had a general intention, which I am sure is quite sensible, of building another railway when and if the circumstances warrant the building of such a railway. The minister says it will be built if there is enough guaranteed traffic or enough guaranteed business to justify the building of the other part of the railway. I sincerely hope the government and the minister are ready to do that for any part of Canada. I mean, that is just nonsense. I mean, if there is enough traffic for it to be a profitable venture for the Canadian National Railways to build a railway anywhere in Canada, the government and the railroad should do it right away. There is no doubt about that. From the way this bill is drafted I think it is just to appease public opinion in this part of Quebec in the lake St. John area. What the government had in mind was to build a railroad from Beattyville to Chibougamau. At the present time the government has no intention of building the eastern part. The government should not be afraid to say so and should not
Canadian National Railways present such phony legislation. That is the reason why I am speaking.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING

Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I could not allow my hon. friend to go unchallenged in connection with the statements he has just made. He made them originally in the course of the general debate when he said that it was not the intention of the government to go on with the complete construction of this railway. May I say that it is, having regard to the circumstances as outlined by the officers of the Canadian National Railways who gave evidence before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. The intention of the Canadian National Railways is quite clear and the intention of the government is equally clear. This is not a matter of two bills, one to build a portion of the line and then to come back later on and build the other portion. It is one bill. This line is considered by the Canadian National Railways and by the government not as two separate projects but as a whole line, the western half of it being built immediately because of the guarantees that have been forthcoming, and the eastern half to be built just as soon as the guarantees are forthcoming. I hope-and in fact it looks as though the assurances will be forthcoming-that the traffic guarantees will permit of the construction of the line as soon as possible after the first half is completed. When my hon. friend says that this is phony legislation, that it is queer legislation and that the government has no intention of going on with the construction of the line, I must say to him that such is not the case at all. I am sure that the House of Commons would not want responsible officers of the Canadian National Railways to come forward with the explanation which they gave in the committee and not be sincere. I am sure that the House of Commons would not believe that they would act in that fashion.
Then there is another statement my hon. friend has made with which I take issue. He said that by constructing first the western half of this line, namely that part which extends from Beattyville to Chibougamau, the effect would be the draining of Quebec traffic out of the province of Quebec into Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext: If I may, I should like to carry on with my argument, because I think it has some bearing certainly on what other hon. members have said. It has a great bearing on my position in the House of Commons. When the officers of the Canadian National Railways dealt with the Ontario line, with the lake Manitouwadge line, and when they explained to the committee that a great deal of the traffic, if not all of it, comprising the concentrates of the mines in the province of Ontario would be fed by this line of the Canadian National Railways into the smelters at Noranda, I did not hear any member from the province of Ontario rise and take any objection to Ontario traffic moving down in to the province of Quebec; nor, for that matter, did I hear any member from the city of Toronto do so. On the contrary, I have had members from the city of Toronto say to me that they are delighted that such is the case. After all, we do not build railway lines in any particular region for limited reasons. Railway lines are built for the development of the country as a whole. That is all the officers of the Canadian National Railways had in mind when they proceeded to recommend to the government the construction of this line of railway which should be considered as a whole line and not as two lines.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is one statement made by the minister which conveys an impression that is hardly in accordance with what the record shows. He says that this bill is in its wording similar to other bills dealing with construction of this kind. However, there is a great difference. In the case of the bill approving of the construction from Terrace to Kitimat there was a definite time limit of construction to be finished in the present [DOT] year. I believe the total time was just over two years. In other 

similar cases, instead of ten years the time provided is normally two years. In construction of this kind there would seem to be no reason why that is not the figure that might very well be used here. Neither from the record of the committee nor in what I have heard here has there been suggested any reason why a ten-year figure should be included in this case. The statement is made that the construction of the Beattyville-Chibougamau line is going to proceed right away. If that is so, why have a ten-year period for that? And most certainly why have the further provision that it should be left until such later date? It is obvious that it is not intended that this provision should apply to the Beattyville-Chibougamau part of the road. From what the minister has said I think it is clear that this provision applies to the construction from St. Felicien to Chibougamau.
That being so, the question then arises as to why we should extend an already very long postponement to 1964 by a still further possibility of postponement. The government either intends that this line be constructed or it does not. The minister has said he hopes that there will be assurances from those who would use this line and that with those assurances construction would proceed. I need not remind him that the line in Ontario which will have a business connection with the Beattyville-Chibougamau road, the Ontario Northland Railway, was built as a development road. It was built with confidence in the future and with the expectation that the resulting development would justify the expenditure. It seems to me that the St. Felicien-Chibougamau part of the construction forms an essential link in this whole development. As the minister has said, concentrates from Ontario will move into the mill at Noranda. Certainly no one is raising any question about that. That is a very good balance of interest in this matter. It would also seem there are obvious advantages in completing the link and in having a road that will run right through St. Felicien to Noranda and on into northern Ontario so that these areas are connected by that road.
I would not wish to have it suggested that in supporting this amendment I do so with any idea that further representations should be made. I think this is an essential part of the whole construction. The date of 1964 set out in the bill is already too far away, but at least if a date ten years away is going to be placed in the act there can be no such reason as would ordinarily apply to extend that date still further. The reason I support the amendment is simply that I believe this

work should proceed now as part of the construction and as part of the network of rail lines which will open up that whole area.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition asked why there is a distinction between this bill apd the other bills. Of course one must remember that the other lines were much shorter than this one. This line is 294 miles in length and if you add the Ontario mileage plus the mileage from Cache lake to Chibougamau you have construction of something over 300 miles in length. When you compare that with the 46 or 47-mile line from Terrace to Kitimat and the somewhat longer line from Kiask Falls to Barraute that explains to some extent the difference.
I would not want the committee to think for one moment that Canadian National Railways or, for that matter, the government, feel that the railway should take powers which parliament thinks they should not take. It was the feeling of the Canadian National Railways that because of all the circumstances they should have a ten-year period, and the bill was drafted with the provisions that were mentioned earlier and such as are to be found in the other bills.
But if the committee feels that this is taking powers that should not be taken and if it will please the committee I have no objection to accepting the amendment as it has been moved and leaving it to the Canadian National Railways to build the three lines, or two lines rather-I will put it that way-from now until 1964 in the hope that they will find sufficient guarantees during that period to be able to continue the extension from St. Felicien to Chibougamau. If that will meet the pleasure of the committee then perhaps I can accept the amendment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

In welcoming acceptance of the amendment that has been moved, I do want to mention one thing. Mr. Chairman, on my return from a journey last week to the riding I have the honour to represent in this house, I was told of the discussions that took place here on second reading of the bill authorizing the construction of a railway line to the mining district of Chibougamau, and I would not like to let this opportunity slip by without voicing my humble contribution, as this question is of great importance to my constituents.
I read the remarks made by the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) during that debate, and I am very much surprised at the unfair accusations of partiality which were levelled against him later. Since my election as member for Roberval, I have asked the help of the hon. Minister of Transport in many circumstances, in the interests of my county. I even had occasion to introduce two delegations to him, and he welcomed them with true understanding; I am certain that my constituents are in a position to appreciate his frankness, his courtesy and his kindness to them, and I say
[Mr. Gagnon. J

that, just as I have every confidence in the minister, their trust in him remains unchanged, for they know the facts, and are able to view the situation objectively.
The future of the county of Roberval, for instance, is dependent upon the decisions which the Department of Transport will take with regard to this Chibougamau railway. My colleague from Lake St. John (Mr. Gauthier) and myself have put this view on record in this house, and mentioned it a sufficient number of times to the appropriate department for this principle to have been embodied in a bill, such as is now the case. That is one of the reasons why the electors of the constituency of Roberval preferred putting their trust in a government supporter, knowing full well that his actions on their behalf would be more effective. Events have proven them right, and will certainly continue to do so. That is, after all, the important thing. I am not here to attack the government which my electors have given me a clear mandate to support. I am here to protect my constituents' interests and even those of the people of Chicoutimi, although, in order to do so, I will have to repudiate certain statements made by the member for that constituency (Mr. Gagnon). The member for Chicoutimi is an independent, and doubtless acts independently of the progress of his constituency if we are to go by certain of his diplomatic absences on the attendance of certain important delegations which have come here to make representations in connection with the Chibougamau-Lake St. John railway, more particularly that of March 1953, or again if we go by the fact that he had remained absolutely silent on this matter until such time as, desiring to show himself under his true colours, he rushed headlong into indiscriminate criticism. He has attempted to make a bugbear of the neighbouring province in order to make us forget his past inertia and biased arguments, now that he has made up his mind to wake up and concern himself with this all-important matter. Such attempts to take credit for something done by others is what we can really expect of these so-called independents.
My colleague from Lake St. John and myself have never stopped concerning ourselves with this vital matter of a railway connecting the mining district of Chibougamau to that of lake St. John. We have obtained from the government as well as from the Canadian National Railways sufficient guarantees to cause us to remain optimistic with regard to the ultimate implementation of this

project which is very close to our hearts and to those of our constituents, for a number of reasons.
Even though the amendment proposed to Bill 442, in the railway committee, by my colleague from Lake St. John and myself was defeated, we remain confident that the Chibougamau-St. Felicien stretch of railway will be built within a reasonable length of time and we would ask the Minister of Transport to continue his sympathetic support, even though some eleventh hour converts should continue their pessimistic pronouncements, thus showing how certain all-important considerations escape them in this connection.

Otherwise, if they keep on thinking only of financial guarantees,
Canadian National Railways it means that this government is interested only in finding new markets, new outlets, for the Canadian National Railways, and not primarily in the industrial "development" of a district. And as the minister surely does not intend to confine himself solely to a consideration of the dollars and cents that the Chibougamau-St. Felicien line will yield during its first year of operation, he must first of all consider what measure of development would be brought about in the Saguenay district. I feel there is no doubt as to that. This is the reason for my urging the government to support this amendment, so that both sections of the railway may be built now.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order may I remind the hon. member that if he had listened to the speech I delivered before he extended congratulations to the government on its attitude and decision to build this railway, he would have noted that I said then that we would start building the Beattyville-Chibougamau section before the St. Felicien section. The hon. member would, at that time, have extended his congratulations and his thanks to this government on its decision to build the western section before the eastern section.

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
The minister took good care not to tell us that the second part of the project would be undertaken only in ten years, or even more, from now. And, according to the second part of this bill, or at least according to section 1, it is possible that that part of the project may never be undertaken, and that is the whole problem, as the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Girard) has pointed out.
One must not always live in the hope of making money; the main thing is to be an optimist. And if the government of the province of Quebec had not anticipated that large mineral deposits could be mined in that area between St. Felicien and Chibougamau, it certainly would not have spent millions and millions on the development of that area.
I want to protest also against this bill because the government's stand on the matter will encourage the shipping of Quebec's natural resources to another part of Canada, and that will be detrimental to the population of that province. I find rather strange the stand taken by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Villeneuve) who, a moment ago, was rather optimistic and expressed such confidence in the government that he was even ready to give it a blank cheque. Well, Mr. Chairman, I am not ready to give such a blank cheque to the government, especially when it introduces a motion which says one thing and a bill which says practically the opposite. I say that the part of this line which, under the circumstances, looks to me to be the more important one is the section which runs from St. Felicien to Chibougamau, and, consequently, I shall vote for the amendment presented by the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon).

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
Before the [DOT]question is put on this amendment, I would just like to point out, as I did in committee, that I propose to support the amendment. I have twice, in this house, asked that both sections be built simultaneously, and the proposed change being along these lines, I shall support it. I must say that, like my hon.


friend from Roberval (Mr. Villeneuve), we on this side of the house put our trust in the government, and that the people of Quebec province share this confidence.

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext: We shall know at the next election.

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext: As I said, that is why we need not worry about the next election, and we trust that the Saguenay district will also put its confidence in the government, because, by then, we will have our railway. If it is not then completed, it should at least be well on its way.

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to mention that I feel the same way as my hon. friend from Lake St. John with regard to the government, and that I shall also vote for the amendment. I want to tell the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne) that neither he, nor our friends opposite are going to build this railway; it is going to be built by the government through the Canadian National.
I am convinced that will be done soon and that is why I have shown much optimism and have thanked once more the minister for the consideration he has shown and still shows for the population of my riding of Roberval.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (for ihe Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act to provide for the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of death benefits up to a maximum of five thousand dollars for the spouse, or the estate
(a)	of a public servant.
(b)	of a member of the regular forces, or in certain circumstances,
(c)	of a former public servant, or
(d)	of a former member of the regular forces, where the public servant, member of the regular forces, former public servant or former member of the regular forces has paid contributions into the consolidated revenue fund.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext: Is the parliamentary assistant going to give an explanation of this resolution?

speakeroldname: Mr. W. M. Benidickson (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext:
The
bill to be founded on this resolution will provide a scheme of contributory death benefits which will supplement the other benefits already provided in the Public Service Superannuation Act. In the case of members of the regular armed forces, it will provide similar death benefits to supplement the other benefits provided under the Defence Services Pension Act. The benefit will be payable in the form of a lump sum to the spouse of the contributor or, if there is no surviving spouse, to the estate of the deceased. It is designed to provide funds immediately to cover the inevitable expenses arising out of or consequential upon the last illness and death of the contributor.
As the resolution indicates, it will be possible for a participant in this plan to elect to participate after retirement, provided that he regularly makes the required contributions.
I do not think that I need say more about the details of the proposed bill at this stage. Because of its nature the Minister of Finance thinks that the most effective way to deal
Public Service Superannuation Act with the details of the bill will be to refer it to the banking and commerce committee for study and report after second reading, and he proposes to make that motion at the proper time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure we
appreciate the proposal that after second reading this bill will be referred to the committee on banking and commerce. I believe the committee will generally approve of that way of dealing with this legislation. The fact that it will go straight from second reading to the committee on banking and commerce means that this is the only opportunity, before it goes before that committee, for questions to be asked and answered here on the floor of the house.
I realize that we sometimes have a little difficulty getting all the information we should like at this stage as to the details of a bill to be introduced after the resolution has been passed, but it does seem to me that the nature of this proposal is such that there are one or two questions which the parliamentary assistant might answer more specifically. I note that the resolution does give one figure, namely, $5,000, as the maximum amount of a death benefit which is available under this legislation. Can he indicate what formula the government has in mind on the basis of which that $5,000 maximum is reached or on the basis of which any lesser amount is the maximum in the case of other participants? Can he also indicate what the contribution, or the premium payable under this legislation, is to be? It seems quite clear from the resolution that the legislation envisages the making of payments into a fund by civil servants or by members of the regular forces, receiving in turn the protection or the benefit of a payment at death either to the spouse of the participant or to the estate.
Our views on the matter might of course be affected by the amounts to be paid in and the corresponding benefits to be received, but generally speaking this proposal looks good to us. I find myself in the position where I have to say almost exactly the same thing I said yesterday with respect to another matter which the same parliamentary assistant was piloting through the house. To the extent that this is good for civil servants we think it is good for Canadians generally. It looks to me that what is being provided is a form of life insurance, term insurance, and very good protection too. Although the figures are not in the bill as to what it will cost, my guess is that it would be much less costly, indeed considerably less costly, than would be the case if the same kind of insurance were purchased from private insurance companies. I can well remember the hue and cry that has been raised in the

Public Service Superannuation Act newspapers and in some quarters in the country when on occasion we have suggested there might be room for improvement in the field of life insurance if it were handled on a government basis rather than on a private basis. But here it is. It is for a select group; it is just for civil servants; but if I read this resolution aright, it is a form of socialized life insurance. It is restricted to one form of life insurance, namely, term policies, which incidentally life insurance companies do not peddle very zealously. But to that extent I suggest it is all to the good, and I hope the parliamentary assistant will answer some of these questions now, bearing in mind the fact that we will not have a chance to ask questions when we are on second reading, and after that the bill will go to the committee.
I should also be glad if the parliamentary assistant would elaborate on his statement as to the possibility of civil servants who are now retired coming under this plan. If they do elect to come under it, what amounts will they have to pay in order to get the benefits? May I ask also whether the benefit provided under this arrangement, or under this term insurance policy, is a fixed benefit, or does it go up or down with the passage of time or with the advance in years of the participant? A colleague of mine suggests that I use the words "the insured". The point is well taken. The resolution refers to these people as participants, but in point of fact they are being insured under this government scheme. I should like to reserve final comment until we have all the details, but on the basis of such details as I can get from this resolution, it looks very good. My hope is that a plan of this nature, good as it is, will before long be available not only to civil servants but to all the citizens of Canada at the same relatively low cost at which I am satisfied the government is in a position to make this insurance available.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext: Would the parliamentary assistant prefer to have me defer my questions until he has answered the previous questions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext: Go ahead.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext:
Then I shall ask my questions now. I listened with interest to the inferences that have been drawn by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, which I have no doubt he has been glad to draw and which the rest of us will have to ponder.
Is this compulsory? When I say "compulsory" I mean for everybody. For instance, does it apply to bachelors and others who may need no death allowances? Secondly,


has there been any contact with representatives of the service forces and of the civil servants to see what their attitude is? One has heard of instances here and there of people who did not like the compulsory feature. Would there be anything in the operation of the act, in so far as the superannuation or the pension benefits are concerned, which would indicate that there was any substantial measure of opposition or discontent in that the measure would also be compulsory? These are the questions I should like to ask, and in particular I should like to know whether any means has been taken to sound out the views of the proposed beneficiaries.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are one or two questions I would like to ask in connection with this resolution. I presume it is of a compulsory nature for all members of the civil service and the armed forces and for that reason I have certain qualms as to whether it is highly desirable that we should compel members of the civil service and the armed forces to take out this kind of insurance.
There are large numbers of persons in the civil service and armed forces who have for years contributed to various life insurance schemes and have provided themselves with such security as they feel necessary or desirable for the safeguarding of their families after death. Are they now to be compelled to take out another $5,000 worth of life insurance which may place considerable hardship upon them, and hardship particularly in the case of a widow? For this additional $5,000 would be subject to succession duties if the estate was such that the succession duties had to be paid.
Then, will it also apply to the female members of the civil service and the armed forces? Many of these young ladies who are in the civil service and in the armed forces would I think prefer to take out an annuity rather than life insurance. They regard the responsibility of providing for their families, should they marry, as the responsibility of their future husbands, whereas if they are single and intend to remain so then they would much rather have security in their old age in the form of an annuity rather than life insurance.
Is there any means in this scheme by which the life insurance could be commuted in old age and used to look after their needs after they have retired from the service and have reached old age?
Now, regarding the paragraph dealing with former public servants and members of the armed forces, does that refer to personnel who have already retired, or only to such personnel as those who will not have

completed their payments up to the maximum of $5,000 and then will be able to make contributions after they have retired? Also, is there any intention of extending this scheme to crown corporations, and does this scheme also include members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, several questions have been raised and probably I should deal with them in the order presented. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre raised the question of the amounts and the reason for selecting these amounts. The maximum is set out in the resolution and it will be $5,000, but it will be $5,000 or a year's salary, whichever is the lesser amount. That is the manner in which the figure has been arrived at. It is proposed that all people who are contributors under the Civil Service Superannuation Act will be contributors under this scheme, and the reason for that is that when everyone is in a group scheme the rate is much lower.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext:
The rate proposed will be 40 cents per month per thousand which, as hon. members will recognize, is a pretty low rate of insurance.
Questions in regard to the compulsory feature of the scheme were raised by the hon. member for Greenwood and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, and one of them raised the point of a bachelor not desiring to take out insurance payable on his death and probably not having any close relative to whom he wished the benefits to pass. However, as I indicated in my statement, this is not intended to create an estate. It is primarily intended to take care of the expenses which normally are connected with death, and particularly if death is preceded by an illness. That, of course, would apply to the single person in the same manner as to the married person.
Then, the cost is much lower if everyone in the group participates, because hon. members will recognize that the group will then include the old and the young, the healthy and those who have not good health.
In the case of the bachelor, he might while a bachelor decline to take insurance but then in a few years he may change his status and be very glad to come into the scheme. If that was left optional hon. members can see the kind of difficulties which would arise by allowing such people to remain outside the scheme. It would not be fair to the original participant to allow these people who have had second thoughts to come in probably at
Public Service Superannuation Act a time when it was strictly to their advantage and when they would lessen the advantage to those who were in the scheme from the very beginning.
The reference I made to the possibility of continuing to participate was not necessarily applicable to a civil servant after retirement. A provision would be made to allow persons who had participated over a certain number of years in the scheme to continue with their payments even if they were leaving for other employment. Similarly, it is expected that where the crown corporations have a desire to allow their staffs to participate, arrangements will be made to provide for that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext:
Before the parliamentary
assistant leaves that point, do I understand from what he has just said that any former civil servant now retired on superannuation would not have the opportunity to elect for this scheme?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext: No, there is no opportunity for someone who has retired. Then, I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre overlooked the point that we already have under the Civil Service Insurance Act an optional insurance scheme, though only a portion of the members of the civil service have taken advantage of that act. From now on, there will no longer be an opportunity to take out insurance under that scheme, and it is expected that this scheme will take the place of the other one.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext:
May I ask
the parliamentary assistant whether the government will contribute in the same way as those who are members of the scheme? In other words, will the government be contributing 40 cents per month per thousand?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext: The intention is that the government contribution will be made at the time when the benefit is payable, and they will pay a portion of the benefit. Under, I think, the Civil Service Act, there is a provision whereby, in respect of employees who have had more than two years of service, a gratuity of two months' salary is paid if they die while in the service. The group insurance, of course, will provide a death benefit amounting to a full year's salary, but it will be in substitution of this gratuity which has hitherto been payable by the government.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext:
In other
words, the government will be contributing only on death?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext:
Yes; and of course the government will carry the cost of administration through the insurance department.

speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act to provide for the appointment of more than one deputy commissioner and also to provide for the granting of pensions to certain officers and men not at present eligible.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF MORE THAN ONE DEPUTY COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
I notice that the bill to be based on the resolution deals with the appointment of a deputy commissioner and the matter of the granting of pensions to certain officers and men of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police not at present eligible.

Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act As I know there are a number of what are regarded as anomalies in the present pension situation of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, I think it would be appreciated if the minister would give us a general outline of the scheme of overhaul which is contemplated because that might obviate unnecessary discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF MORE THAN ONE DEPUTY COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with regard to the appointment of the deputy commissioner, the position is that part I of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act provides that the governor in council may by commission appoint a deputy commissioner. This position was established on the first of April, 1932 and since that time, as is obvious to all of us, the responsibilities and the strength of the force have increased greatly. The senior assistant commissioner, under the authority of an order in council dated March 26, 1953, now receives the same rate of pay as that authorized for the deputy commissioner and is performing duties of equal responsibility. We consider that it is desirable to regularize this situation by providing in the establishment for two deputy commissioners and by cancelling the establishment and salary provision of the senior assistant commissioner. There are therefore, as is obvious, no financial implications involved.
With regard to the proposed pension provisions, there are, as hon. members are aware, two separate pension provisions for the force. One is outlined and referred to in parts II and III of the act and represents the original non-contributory pension for which until March 1949 all members of the force had been eligible. Under these parts II and III non-contributory pension members who have completed over ten years service and who have been discharged for inefficiency or misconduct are automatically entitled upon discharge to a pension of one-half of the disability pension ordinarily available to them on retirement until the age of 65, and then two-thirds of such disability pension after that age. In addition, authority is given to increase that amount, if, according to the circumstances of such inefficiency or misconduct, that seems to be desirable, to two-thirds of such disability pension until 65 and the full pension after the age of 65.
In 1949 a new contributory pension scheme was inaugurated in the force which was to be available for all new members of the force who came on strength after that date and to those old members who wished to join the contributory pension fund. It provided a number of additional features such as an allowance to the widow and children of the member, and other features of that sort which


were not formerly available under the noncontributory pension scheme. But in the new contributory pension scheme there was no provision for a pension in the event of the member of the force in this scheme being discharged for inefficiency or misconduct.
Upon further consideration we now think that the position of the pensioner under the two schemes should be equalized in that respect. That is the purpose of the bill to be introduced by the resolution.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF MORE THAN ONE DEPUTY COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext: How many have been discharged for inefficiency or misconduct since 1949?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF MORE THAN ONE DEPUTY COMMISSIONER, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF MORE THAN ONE DEPUTY COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
At the convention of the Canadian Legion in Montreal in 1952 recommendations were made that those members of the force who had served in armed forces during the war other than armed forces raised in Canada should be permitted to count their time towards their pension. I believe that under the old act members of the force who had served with the imperial forces were permitted to count their time in such service towards their pension from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. But when part V was introduced it was limited to those who had served on active service in the naval, military and air forces of His Majesty's forces raised in Canada. That excluded those members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who had served in the imperial forces.
I very much appreciate the traditional Canadian character of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, but ever since the force was formed there has always been a percentage of the men who have seen service in forces of the crown other than those actually raised in Canada. I was wondering whether any provision had been made in these amendments to allow these men with overseas service with forces other than actual Canadian forces in the wars in which Canada has taken part to count that time towards their police pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF MORE THAN ONE DEPUTY COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext: No. The present projected act does not contemplate any amendments other than those which I have mentioned.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF MORE THAN ONE DEPUTY COMMISSIONER, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF MORE THAN ONE DEPUTY COMMISSIONER, ETC.

No. They are, I think, under a proper disability by reason of their misconduct, but it does not seem fair that a man who has served for quite a period of time and who commits some serious item of misconduct, perhaps of a momentary character but which means that he cannot be kept in

the force, should be penalized in respect of his whole accumulated pension. This provision is to meet a case of that kind.

I know that usually retroactive legislation is not to be encouraged, but if it is now ascertained, as the minister says, that it is unfair there should be that discrimination as it were between the two classes, is there any reason why under those circumstances, and after second thought, the provisions of the amendments that will be introduced in consequence of this resolution should not be placed in a position where they would be effectual since 1949.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF MORE THAN ONE DEPUTY COMMISSIONER, ETC.

I should like also to emphasize that research is not a static thing. It is continually changing to meet changing conditions and also, like an organism, must grow from small beginnings. Money will not buy trained men if they are not available, so that in looking at and assessing the growth and development of research in any country, one must always keep in mind that it is a changing picture and that it is often impossible to provide at any moment everything that may be desirable.
I would have you note there, Mr. Speaker, that the minister did say money will not buy trained men. What happened to the men that we did have in this country who were trained at the various wonderful universities we have in Canada? Most of them I dare say-I should not say most of them-have gone south of the border. They find it is more lucrative to enter the scientific field there, especially the field of research. I have spoken to a number of them from time to time, and their contention is that our economic standard is of equal value to that of the United States, and therefore they feel that they should be paid as well as their United States counterparts.
I have no doubt but that the minister feels, and rightfully so, that we are doing everything we can to encourage those individuals to stay here. Now that he has pointedly indicated we are entering the research field on a grandiose scale, we might say, we should invite these young men and women to return. In many instances they have not accepted United States citizenship, and have intimated that they wish to return. Possibly a gesture from our government might lure

British North America Act them back so that we would have them available for research purposes. I would heartily endorse what the research council subscribes to, namely that no brilliant young student should be prevented from receiving training because of lack of scholarships or grants.
In so far as grants are concerned, as a young nation we probably are giving as much as we feel we can afford, but I think that the more money we spend on research, the more results we will have and the greater the number of industries that will be set up. My main concern in this regard, of course, is how do our grants compare with the grants and bursaries given by United States universities? Anyone who has taken a trip to the United States in recent years, I am sure will have discovered there is an increase in the number of requests for information about the vast mineral fields in British Columbia that have been opened up, the oil fields in Alberta and the mining interests in Ontario and Quebec.
