speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE QUORUM OF HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE QUORUM OF HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: If the hon. member speaks now he will close the debate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE QUORUM OF HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I shall be very brief in closing the debate on the second reading of Bill 81, to amend the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1952, with respect to the quorum of the House of Commons. As hon. members are aware, the purpose of this bill is to increase the quorum of the House of Commons.
At the present time, according to section 48 of the British North America Act, the


minimum attendance for the house to transact business is fixed at 20 members. As I have pointed out on previous occasions, there has been no change in that figure since 1867. Since that time, however, there has been a fairly substantial increase in the membership of the house. Originally the membership was 181, whereas our present membership is 265. For my part I feel the quorum should be a much larger figure than that proposed in my bill. However one realizes the difficulty of having changes made, particularly when he is dealing with the British North America Act. Therefore my bill proposes simply that we maintain the same proportion that was established when the quorum was fixed in 1867 at 20 members.
Incidentally, as I pointed out previously, the figure of 20 members was carried forward from the figure which served as the quorum in the legislative assembly of the Province of Canada previous to 1867, when the total of members representing the two parts, Upper and Lower Canada, was considerably fewer. It does seem to me that to maintain that proportion and thereby to increase the quorum to 30 members is the least that we should be doing.
Various arguments have been advanced as to why this should not be done, the chief argument being that there are many committees members have to attend. But I press the point that at no time are there enough committees sitting-in fact there are not either rooms in the building or reporters sufficient to make it possible-to take away enough members to make a quorum of 30 members, or even a much larger number, impossible to attain.
It has been said to me in recent days, on occasions when at one time or another attendance in the house has fallen rather low, that if my bill were to pass it would be that much more difficult to keep the house working. It has been said that it would be more difficult to keep 30 members here than to keep 20. Well, if at times the attendance in the house falls within reach of the minimum fixed by law, that is all the more reason why the minimum should be a little higher than it is at the present time, so that we might have a better attendance at all times.
People outside cannot understand why the quorum is set so low. Some have questioned my bill on the ground that it does not fix a high enough figure. As I have said, I think it should be considerably higher; but surely this is the least that we should approve, namely the maintenance of the same proportion as was established in 1867.
This then is the purpose of my bill. If it were to pass the house and receive approval

in the other place and the assent of His Excellency the Governor General, by virtue thereof the British North America Act would be amended. No further steps would be necessary. This is in consequence of the amendment to that act we obtained in the fall of 1949, as a result of which we now have the right to amend the British North America Act, the constitution of Canada, with respect to matters exclusively federal, by a bill put through the parliament of Canada.
It is in the exercise of that right that this bill is presented, and I believe it would meet with approval outside the house if we were to take this step to increase the minimum attendance required in the house. Therefore, I urge hon. members to adopt the bill, which might now be put to a vote.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 152, REVISED STATUTES OF 1952-VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words in support of the principle of the check-off. It seems to me that in provinces where the principle of the check-off has been applied the ground of difference between employers and employees has been very much narrowed, and that is a condition which should be favoured by anyone in Canada who believes in supporting the best interests of our country.
I am well aware, of course, that there are conditions which do not make this bill as potentially effective in the federal field as would a similar principle applied in the provincial field. But I wish to make it clear that our experience in British Columbia is that since we have had the principle of the check-off available on the basis of a majority vote in any given industry then the relations in key industries such as that at Trail and in other great industrial centres of British Columbia have been greatly improved, and the really marked improvement there has been in the relationships between employer and employee in British Columbia in the past 10 years or so is due to the fact that an enlightened Liberal minister of labour did make certain great improvements in industrial relations. The check-off was one of these reforms which the Liberal minister of labour enacted and I therefore wish to make it very clear, Mr. Speaker, that I am in favour of the check-off and believe it deserves consideration by this house.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 152, REVISED STATUTES OF 1952-VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am very happy indeed to hear the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) expressing himself along the lines on which he has just spoken, and speaking as an hon. member from the province of British Columbia I must say that my own experience in connection with the introduction of this check-off principle confirms what the hon. member has said.
He mentioned that improved industrial relations had resulted in such industrial centres as the city of Trail. Certainly I know that in the coastal areas, where the principle of the check-off has been accepted in the great British Columbia lumber industry, it has certainly served in my opinion to narrow the areas of difference which exist from time to time between employers and employees.
I must confess though that the remarks of the hon. member struck me as being much more in line with the best traditions of Liberalism than have some of the remarks I have heard coming from that side of the house in recent months. Hon. members will no doubt recall that the debate on this particular bill has progressed at a rather

leisurely pace, which may be just as well because it has perhaps allowed some of us who are convinced of the sanity of this measure to cool off a little before making a reply to some of the remarks which have been made. I have before me a record of Hansard containing a speech made by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mrs. Shipley) in which she refers to this bill as "such compulsory legislation as is here proposed." It seems to me that one has only to take that phrase from that particular speech to demonstrate how absurd that contention is.
I would like to add that the remarks I have heard on this bill in the previous discussions seemed to me to be echoing the arguments I heard a number of years ago almost ad nauseam from some of the employing interests who were opposed to the introduction of this principle, and which were based upon the supposition that the working people of this country know nothing about maintaining democracy and are less able to look after their own affairs than the rest of the citizens of this country.
I maintain this is an utterly false assumption. Some of the arguments which have been advanced from that side of the house reminded me, in their reference to certain leaders of the trade union movement, of nothing so much as a Tory attempting to describe the actions of the present Canadian cabinet, and while I might admit that people who become somewhat accustomed to power and responsibility may have a tendency at times to abuse that power, I would submit that that is certainly no more true of the leadership of the trade union movement than it is of the government of Canada. Anyone who keeps these things in perspective and who has a proper sense of proportion in connection with them realizes how absurd those arguments are.
This is an extremely simple arrangement that is suggested. Far from being a proposal for compulsory legislation, it is simply a proposal for permissive legislation. It only means that if a group of workers have decided amongst themselves that they wish to adopt this system, the law says that they shall have the right to do it without having to fight an economic battle with their employer in order to achieve it. That is one of the ways in which the agencies of the various levels of government in this country can help to reduce the area of conflict that exists between the various groupings in our society.
I suggest that it is something that we have in many fields within the provinces today and certainly the experience we have had there has been good, in my opinion. Even the new labour act which was introduced

recently by the present government of British Columbia-much as I disagree with many of the sections in it-did not seek to eliminate this particular type of provision. I suggest that there certainly can be no harm in this parliament's setting an example to the people in all parts of the country with regard to allowing this form of democratic right to the workers of Canada.

The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has, I think, stated his position with regard to it.
Industrial Relations
May I just remind the house that this is a matter which has been before parliament on a number of occasions. It may seem a bit tedious for me to tell this part of the story again, but I feel that I must remind the members of the house that as long ago as 1948, when the present Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act was first drafted and placed upon our statute books, when that legislation was going through parliament there was one stage at which it had in it the very principle, the very wording, that is contained in the bill that is now before the house. That principle, namely the voluntary revocable check-off, was written into the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act in the committee on industrial relations, on the motion of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). Despite the fact that the voluntary revocable check-off was written into the bill when it was in the committee on industrial relations, when the bill came back into the house an amendment was moved by another Liberal member to strike out that provision. On a division, the provision was lost in the committee of the whole house. Since that time this identical bill has been before the house a number of times. The votes have varied. The last time that the matter came to a vote was in 1951 when some 67 votes were cast in favour of it, including 17 on the Liberal side of the house, and all those on the opposition side who were present at the time. That was the largest number we have yet obtained by way of a vote in favour of this bill. I hope that today it might be larger, and that one of these days we may win the acceptance of this principle.
May I remind hon. members of the house again that what we are asking in this bill is not a compulsory measure. Rather we are asking for the very minimum of union security, namely the voluntary revocable checkoff. The provision would be that in any case where a union is recognized as the bargaining unit for a group of employees, it would be the right of any employee in that union to request in writing that his dues to the union be deducted at the source and be paid over to the union by his employer. It would be the further right of such employee to revoke that request at any time. In other words, Mr. Speaker, as others have pointed out-indeed others on both sides of the house-this is the minimum form of union security that can be written into any labour legislation. It seems to me that the least this parliament should do is to accent this minimum form of union security and make it the law for those who come under federal labour jurisdiction.
I remind hon. members that in a number of the provinces of this country there is in

I also remind hon. members that in 1953 when this bill was before parliament there was made an amendment that it be not read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the committee on industrial relations. That committee considered the subject matter carefully and in its report indicated its endorsation of the principle. That was the position taken by that committee, with the additional recommendation that the matter be studied by the government in its review and proposed revision of the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. That stand taken by the committee was confirmed by the house when the committee's report was made to the House Of Commons. That then is the last position taken by parliament, namely endorsation of the principle of the voluntary revocable check-off and a recommendation that the matter be considered by the government.
I suppose the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration feels that it is a case of carrying out that recommendation for this consideration to go on. But some of us-including labour generally-feel that there comes a time when action is required rather than just the promise of still further consideration. When this matter was before the house several months ago I was ready to agree to the request of the Minister of Labour that it stand over for still further consideration to be given to it. That was in addition to the consideration given from the time the report was made to parliament in the last session- over a year ago-through the period between sessions and through the time of the election. In addition to all of that, we have given this additional time since this bill was introduced on December 11, and I think the time has come for the house to decide on the principle itself. In my view this house should now support the principle of the voluntary revocable check-off of trade union dues by voting for this bill.

Mr. Speaker, in dealing with this third instalment of my speech I have only a few more observations to make along the lines I had followed earlier, when I had made reference to getting our young scientists and students back from the United States and other foreign lands to reinterest them in the research work we propose to carry on in this country.
The cost of living is about the same in the United States as in Canada. Wages paid to our industrial workers are about the same, and certainly neither the government nor anyone connected with it should claim we cannot afford to pay these scientists the same amount for the research work we expect them to do as they are being paid by similar organizations in the United States. I would go so far as to say that it seems quite likely at this time that the United States might attribute its success to the fine work its research scientists have done in the last several years; and if one were to check into the persons who are probably responsible for that in all likelihood he would find that a good many of our young Canadian men and women have been responsible to a great extent for that success.
I should like now to leave that field of discussion and turn to one or two statements made by the minister with respect to expenditures made in 1938 and 1939. Industry in the United States spent three or four times the amount spent by the United States government on research. From a standpoint of comparison, the Canadian government spent twice as much as was spent by industry in this country for that purpose. This is a very commendable fact, and those in Canada who are responsible for it should feel quite proud that our government saw fit to spend that much on research, as compared with the amount spent by industry.
Research Council Act
One fact should be kept in mind, however, and that is that a good many of the industries to which reference was made, including such companies as Northern Electric and Westinghouse, have their main offices in the United States. Probably they did not feel they were justified in setting up huge research laboratories in Canada when they could use the knowledge they gained from their Canadian scientists in the United States and pass that knowledge on to their Canadian counterparts.
When one turns to the problem facing the research council today he must see at once the tremendous field offered by the coal industry. I do not wish to spend much time discussing this subject, because all hon. members are aware of the necessity of trying to get our coal industry back on a sound financial basis. It is a fact that not so many years ago we were proud of the fact and, indeed, announced it to the world, that in Canada we had one-seventh of the world's total coal resources. That fact gave us considerable comfort. What should have proved to be one of the greatest assets has, in the hands of this government, turned out to be one of its biggest headaches.
Possibly one of the reasons for this is that we have not done sufficient work in our research laboratories in connection with the utilization of coal. It may be urged that other countries have not spent enough time in discovering a complete utilization of coal, and that their industry has lagged, as well. However, when in trying to excuse ourselves we accuse somebody else we do not give ourselves any legitimate reason for our action. I would ask the research council, through its laboratories, to find more uses for coal so that we may utilize our supply to the fullest extent.
In my correspondence with the research council I have noticed that there is a reasonable amount of co-ordination between laboratories under government jurisdiction and research facilities set up by industry. This is to be commended, and as a result excellent work is being done. I sometimes wonder however whether we have not gone too far in accepting the statements of research laboratories. My view is that we should have a closer check-up to see whether those laboratories are telling the truth. I think more particularly of some of the highly advertised soap products offered for sale in Canada today. We hear of one soap advertised as being 99-44/100 per cent pure, and apparently the claim is made because this soap floats. This does not mean that it is particularly pure; yet the manufacturer is

permitted to advertise this product as being pure, and the reason given for its purity is that it floats.
Then we have other claims such as, "It makes clothes whiter"; and another soap that "Duz everything". And so on, down through the list. I come to a comparatively new product in connection with a certain type of clothing advertised in Ottawa. I have reference to dacron, which is another form of nylon, and also to orlon. We have several different types of materials made of these synthetic substances; but there is no guarantee as to what value there is in these products. There is a good deal of indiscriminate advertising with respect to them. Our research council has not indicated whether these are or are not good products.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the amendments to the national Research Council Act are more or less formal, this debate gives us an opportunity to consider the extent of this parliament's responsibility in matters of research. It is interesting to note in the estimates this year the extent of the funds which are voted for research. In the Department of Agriculture votes 5 to 15 deal with the science service of that department, and they call for just short of $10 million; in the same department the experimental farm service calls for just over $10 million. Then, in the Department of Fisheries votes 144 to 147 deal with the fisheries research board and call for expenditures of $2,500,000. In the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources vote 329 deals with the forestry branch and, together with the grants to universities for research work, amounts to $1 million. Then of course there is a very large item appropriated for the national defence research board amounting to over $50 million, and we have not yet come to the main agency of research, namely, the national research coun- [DOT] cil, which is listed for $16,081,000. Following that is the atomic energy control board which has $13,500,000 assigned to it. These figures amount to a total of over $105 million, which is to be voted by this parliament for purposes of research. One cannot help but be impressed with the extent of the research work which is the responsibility of this parliament.
In making these remarks tonight I do not approach the work of any of our agencies in a critical or complaining frame of mind.
I believe that we are being well served by the agencies in their respective spheres. I believe the national research council might well consider expending a larger proportion of its budget in grants to universities. My opinion is that to some extent universities, in which much of the actual research work must be done, are cramped for funds which they receive through grants from the national research council, and that perhaps a larger proportion of the budget could usefully be used in that direction. But what impresses one most, Mr. Speaker, is the opportunity that this country offers for research which would be beneficial. It would not be possible to overestimate the importance to Canada of efficient and active research agencies directed towards the maintenance of the

enviable position which Canada has attained today in the world as the third trading nation of the world, in which the material equipment for life and the pursuit of happiness are equal to those of any other country of the world.
We have attained that enviable position through the initiative and enterprise of our people, largely our inventive people and research workers. If we are to proceed from the point we have reached, which I describe as an enviable point, and maintain our position, it seems to me that we must never let that vital spark to this kind of society die down.
We have recognized the needs of underdeveloped and less privileged countries in various ways and are aiding them with very large sums of money, such as the vote for the Colombo plan, to which we are devoting $25 million a year. The difference between such countries and Canada is largely accounted for by the application of ingenuity to the material things that we have and from which we build up our comfort and maintenance in an industrial society.
Canada itself, Mr. Speaker, is an underdeveloped country, and we shall go forward from our present position at a rate which will largely be conditioned by the efficiency and efficacy of our research service. If one looks back over recent history I think it is clear that no one fifty years ago in his best imaginative moments would have conjured up a vision of the society in which we live today. There have been so many changes in the mechanical field that anyone fifty years ago attempting to forecast the life of this country which we enjoy today would have been completely at a loss to foretell what was ahead. I can see that in the future the same relative changes will take place but probably at an accelerated pace. We are living in an age of great speed, and it may be that those of us here tonight, if we were to try to foretell what society in Canada would be like, even fifteen years from now, would be very wide of the mark. What it will be like will largely depend on the efforts of the scientists.
What I wish to direct attention to tonight, Mr. Speaker, is the responsibility of this parliament to see that the best is being done, the best use is being made of the public funds which are devoted to that end. It may be instructive, or at least interesting, to recall what was done in the province of Ontario in recent years with a view to assuring the legislature that it was making proper use of the public funds which it had voted for research purposes. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), who was then premier of Ontario, instituted an inquiry in 1945 83276-322
Research Council Act
under the public inquiries act by a volunteer commission of industrial, scientific, professional and union representatives who were interested in this project, under the name of the Ontario research commission. Its terms of reference were to review the research agencies which existed in the province and the expenditures which were being made to see what overlapping there was, what conflict, what gaps and generally to see what could be done to co-ordinate the work of those various agencies and to make the best use of the funds which were being voted for this purpose.
These agencies consisted of federal agencies with which we are all familiar, the departments of the provincial government, many of whom had research agencies, the universities and the agricultural schools, industry with its private research laboratories and the Ontario research foundation, which was a joint enterprise of government and industry financed by the two many years ago, and doing a sort of custom research work for industry.
In the course of their inquiries they came to some conclusions which were reported and embodied in legislation in 1948 which I had the honour of having some part in. The Ontario research council act which was passed in that year, set up a council whose responsibilities, I believe, can best be described in the words of the Ontario research council's annual report for 1952-53. This report was issued after the council had been in operation for five years, first under the chairmanship of Dr. R. C. Wallace for a number of years, and latterly under the chairmanship of Dr. R. K. Stratford, who is scientific adviser to Imperial Oil Limited.
This report describes the four main interests and activities of the council with which I shall deal briefly. The first one was to provide scholarships, because it was recognized that research can be done only where there are trained personnel competent to undertake the work. Paralleled with the scholarships of the national research council some $50,000 a year was devoted to scholarships and, in view of the remarks of the previous speaker, it is interesting to note that these scholarships have not been used to train scientists to emigrate to the United States, and that the men who were trained in scientific research methods by these scholarships are, for the most part, now engaged in scientific work in the Dominion of Canada. I have not the figures at hand, but I believe some 166 out of over 200 persons who benefited by these scholarships are doing the work for which they were specially trained.
5082	HOUSE OF
Research Council Act
The second feature ol the council's responsibility was that of correlating government research efforts in the province in order to ensure a balance with the needs of the various natural resources. It was intended from the beginning that assistance in each important field of research should be given by an advisory committee representing all the active interests and agencies. These committees were to serve as a medium for discussion and closer co-operation between already well-established research agencies. In addition, the advisory committees would be responsible for initiating further research needed in their respective fields. This might be indicated by problems requiring immediate solution, by future long-term needs, or suggested by research developments elsewhere.
In pursuance of that purpose the council's eight advisory committees are now functioning in various areas of natural and physical sciences. These are agriculture, forestry, fisheries and wild life, highways, industrial research, industrial waste, mines and metallurgy, and aerial surveys. The advisory committees have been very effective in bringing together industrial, governmental, and university research people to examine the problems and supervise programs of research.
By way of illustration, Mr. Speaker, may I refer to the work of one of these eight committees I have mentioned to indicate how such an advisory committee may eliminate overlap, may bring all the workers in one particular field of research together so they are aware of what the others are doing, and so that you do not have two or three working on the same problem leaving other problems completely untouched.
For example, the agricultural research committee is convened three or four times a year, has several subcommittees, and is composed of leading research workers in agriculture, not only in the dominion Department of Agriculture, but also in the Ontario department of agriculture, the Ontario School of Agriculture, the Ontario federation of agriculture, the Hydro Electric Power Commission, the Ontario Veterinary College and so on; there are some 18 or 20 different men whose work is in this research field and who come together periodically to review what is being done in that field, and what work is being carried out in that field by the various agencies.
The third purpose of the council is the establishment of grants in aid to encourage industry to combine to solve problems affecting an industry, and which operates somewhat in the manner of the research organizations to which the Minister of Trade
[Mr. Mlchener.I

and Commerce (Mr. Howe) referred when he spoke of such bodies in Great Britain, though on a smaller scale.
Only two of these projects have been undertaken in Ontario. One is a forest research project at Heron Bay, Ontario, where the Ontario Paper Company Limited and the Abitibi Power and Paper Company Limited are co-operating in a silvicultural program with the provincial government. The other one is in the field of air and water pollution in the Sarnia area where five companies are co-operating with the research council in a study which is under the direction of the council's committee on industrial waste. Here I must emphasize again that this advisory group is a voluntary organization of men who may be described as leaders in our industrial life, particularly in its scientific aspects.
The fourth project which they considered to be essential was that of making known the information which is being accumulated by scientists and researchers, particularly to the smaller industries. It is astonishing to note how much of the industry of this country is carried on by smaller groups which employ 50 men or less. In fact 94 per cent of the industries in Ontario employ 50 persons or less and account for 30 per cent of the province's production. That may not pertain throughout Canada but it does indicate that these smaller industries are in the greatest need of information to guard against obsolescence and backwardness in the industrial struggle, because they are not always aware of what is available for them.
I know that on a national scale there is a great accumulation of information and the Ontario agency, in co-operation with the national research council and its technical branch, have established an information service whose sole duty it is to provide information to these smaller industries so that the best use is made of what is known. It is astonishing how much useful information is already available to these industries which could be put to use and profit in cutting down the cost of production if it were only realized and made available.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have only to apply this excursion into what was done in Ontario to our own situation throughout the dominion. The example I have given demonstrates the effort made by a legislature to see that the best use is made of its research dollars, and I think we should ask ourselves some questions along these lines when we come to deal with the expenditure of $105 million, which is not the entire budget, and

in the expenditures which are being made in other fields in order to see that we are getting the best value, whether there is any overlapping in research, whether there is any waste, and whether there are any gaps to be filled.
It seems to me that that is the area with which parliamentary inquiry should periodically concern itself. I appreciate that the amendment has been ruled out of order and I am speaking in more general terms, but I do suggest that this parliament would be well advised to review periodically what is being done with these research dollars to see that the best value is being obtained. We should ask ourselves whether the national research council as at presently constituted is the right body to co-ordinate the work being done by the various agencies. We should also bear in mind that the national research council is spending $16 million out of $105 million and is therefore by no means the only agency engaged in research which is responsible to this parliament. We should also ask ourselves whether it is the right body to advise parliament as to its over-all needs and expenditures for research.
I suggest that the members of this house should be sure that we are making the most of our research brains and agencies. Let us be sure that there are no duplications. Let us be sure what more there is that can be done. A review such as I have suggested would give assurance to the members of this house that they are making the best use of the money which is voted for research purposes. As I have said, this research plays a vital part in the future of this country if it is not only to maintain the position it has but to remain in the forefront of industrial nations.

Before the question is put, Mr. Speaker, I think there are several remarks I might be able to make which would perhaps sum up the interesting and useful debate that we have had on the second reading of this bill. First of all I should like to thank the hon. members who have taken part in this debate for the interest they have shown in the important matter of research and for the contributions they have made by their comments. The speeches we have heard indicate not only the importance to this country of research but also the opinion held by many hon. members of this house with respect to that importance and the need for parliament to discharge, with care and attention, its responsibilities in connection with research.

Research Council Act
I thought that the speeches of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and of the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener) who has just taken his seat were particularly constructive and helpful. The hon. member for St. Paul's gave an interesting description of some of the work of the Ontario research council. It is true that a number of the provinces have followed the lead given in the wider federal sphere by the national research council and have themselves organized research foundations or councils which have done important and helpful work.	: ,
I should remind hon. members that start-, ing tomorrow the national research council here in Ottawa is holding open house, During this open house the facilities of the council will be open to the public for three days. Members of parliament are particularly invited to come tomorrow afternoon for the opening of the open house and to get: what might be called a preview before the general public are invited. I hope that many members will be able to avail themselves of this opportunity. Any who are not able to come along tomorrow afternoon will be more than welcome during the concluding three days of the week when they can come at any time they wish.
In summing up the debate, Mr. Speaker, I feel that I should refer at some length to the speech made in this debate on Tuesday, May 11, by the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy). The hon. member for Lambton West has shown a great interest in the general over-all question of research and we listened to his speech with considerable interest. The hon. member had placed a resolution on the order paper at the beginning of the session and in his speech he made reference to it. The restriction on time allotted for consideration of private members' resolutions effectively excluded the opportunity for parliament to consider this important question.

Several hon. members have made suggestions with respect to a parliamentary committee to consider the broad question of research and also to consider the operations of

the national research council. I for one did not think that this suggestion, at the time it was made, was a practical one for this session. However, in the past we have had extremely useful committees on matters of this kind. Several sessions ago there was set up a committee specifically on the national research council. In recent years we have had two separate committees which studied the specific fields of research and atomic energy and I think they did extremely useful and worth-while work. I can see no objection to the possibility of there being a parliamentary committee at the next session or at some future session of this parliament if hon. members feel that it would be a constructive and worth-while committee to have, keeping in mind the other business with which parliament must deal.
The hon. member for Lambton West in his speech made a number of general remarks on the importance of research and the care with which we should look into our activities in research. But taken as a whole and eliminating the matters of general interest and that sort of thing, I think his speech comes down to, first, the suggestion that there should be a committee, to which I have referred and, second, a list of questions which he felt should be answered. I think it was the intent of his speech to suggest that they Were questions of a kind that a parliamentary committee should answer and should report upon to the house. These questions are found at page 4630 of Hansard of May 11. The first one is as follows:
Are we doing enough in the way of research In this country, . . .
Then he goes on to elaborate on that basic question. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the committee could sit for a long time and never come up with a better answer than to say: We never can do enough in research. It could never be said that enough is being done in research. The question rather is this: In all the circumstances how much can we usefully do, and are we spending in the best way possible the money which is provided by parliament for research? But to suggest that a parliamentary committee or any other body would ever come to the conclusion that we are doing enough in the field of research is not, I think, very practical. The second question that the hon. member asked is as follows:
Are our universities in a position to continue to provide the trained scientific minds and undertake the fundamental research necessary to assure the continued development and productive expansion of this country?
That, Mr. Speaker, is a very basic question, and I think it touches on what is almost a Unique feature of the research program

carried out by the national research council in this country and to a more limited extent by some of the bodies set up by provincial governments in connection with research. The extent and the development of the program of scholarships and grants which are provided through the national research council to students who are prepared to enter upon scientific studies and to prepare themselves for work as research scientists are quite extraordinary. I think the best way to give the house an idea of the kind of program that the national research council carries out in this field is to quote a part of the annual report of the council for 1952-53. On page 36 of the report there is the following:
The awards branch-
That is the awards branch of the national research council.
-administers scholarships and grants in aid of research awarded annually by the national research council. Scholarships awarded in science and engineering include bursaries, studentships and fellowships which have values of $600, $900 and $1,200 respectively for the academic year, to which a summer supplement of $500 may be added. In addition special scholarships valued at $1,500 per year and post-doctorate overseas fellowships at $2,500 are offered. The council also awards two classes of graduate medical research scholarships which have values of $1,800 to $3,000 for awards involving graduate training, and up to $5,000 for senior awards in advanced research.
Then it goes on to deal with dental research and with post-graduate fellowships and certain important fellowships that are provided out of private funds but are administered by the national research council. This program, as I said, is unique, and it is a program that has been very substantially developed over the last few years. For example, in the fiscal year 1938-39 the total of national research council scholarships and research grants for that year was $81,378. In 1953-54 that total had risen to $1,909,000; in other words, almost $2 million.
This program is being expanded just about as rapidly as the research council can see the possibility of spending this money satisfactorily. In other words, they try to ensure that any promising science student in this country who wishes to follow advanced studies of that kind in order to prepare himself for research or other scientific work is able to do so without difficulty. As has already been said in this debate, the objective of the research council is that no promising science student in this country should have to give up his training because of lack of financial support. It is never possible to say that everything is being done in a field of this kind, but I think that the way in which this program has been developed, the tremendous increase in the annual amounts

expended and the number of young men who have been trained for scientific work in this way is a very great achievement. I can assure hon. members that it is one feature of the council's work that is a source of great pride and satisfaction to the president and members of the council and to all those connected with the council's work.
On that point I was very interested, as I am sure all hon. members were, in the remarks of the hon. member for New Westminster and the hon. member for St. Paul's with respect to the training of scientists in Canada. The program of the national research council is of course intended in the first instance to provide training in Canada wherever that is possible. However, I think it would be unwise, and not the kind of policy that parliament should favour, to exclude training outside this country, if necessary, so that our students can have the benefit of the research facilities and the university and other facilities for study that are available not only in the United States but in England and European countries. The real problem is to get the services of these trained men in Canada when they have completed their training. Everything that is possible is of course done to ensure that they either remain in this country or come back to this country and take jobs either in the government service or in industry.
The third question that the hon. member asked reads as follows:
Would accelerated efforts in the field of industrial research, resulting in new products, new uses for old products, improved techniques that lower production costs, enhance or help us, an exporting nation in ever-increasingly competitive world markets?
The answer to that is yes, and no parliamentary committee is required to provide the answer. It is obvious that the only answer is the short answer, and it is in the affirmative.
The fourth question he asked reads as follows:
Are our present fiscal policies, in relation to research expenditures, adequate to induce private industry to undertake the amount of research that should be undertaken . . .
Then he goes on to refer to the activities of government agencies. The point of the question is: Are the fiscal policies of this country properly designed to provide the utmost incentive to private individuals and private enterprise to undertake research projects both in basic research and in specialized research in their own fields? That, I think, is one of the very fundamental questions in this whole problem, and I cannot help feeling that if the hon. member had really gone into the question of what our fiscal policies are and how they compare with the fiscal policies
Research Council Act
of other countries he would have come to the conclusion that we are doing just about as much as can be done in this field.	,
The hon. member was good enough to indicate that the interest of the government in this particular feature of research programs dates back at least to the budget speech of the Hon. Charles Dunning, which he quoted and put on Hansard. At that time, and up to the budget of 1944, the situation with respect to incentives to industry to make expenditures on research was that current expenditures on research or research facilities were regarded as an element of expense if they could be established as an outlay necessarily incurred for the purpose of earning the income. In other words, if the research expenditure could be shown to be a cost of doing business, then that was a deductible expense and no corporate income tax was chargeable upon it. In so far as capital expenditures were concerned, they were not allowed as deductions and only normal depreciation was permitted.
Now, the result of this was that the cost of laboratories, pilot plants and the like was not exempt and the current expenditures that could not be directly related to earning the firm's income were not deductible. In making his budget speech in this house in 1944, the then minister of finance, the Hon. J. L. Ilsley, said this, as recorded at page 4181 of Hansard for June 26, 1944:
All will agree that Canadian industry must expand its research and technical development if we are to apply the most advanced technical knowledge to our resources, and maintain our competitive position. By all means, let us borrow from whatever is best from other countries, but what we can borrow is not always what we need.
I believe the hon. member will agree that that statement puts into words fairly well what he had in mind in dealing with this subject, the necessity of expanding research and technical development in order to maintain our competitive position. At that time in 1944, Mr. Ilsley and the government were looking forward to the transition from a war to a peacetime economy, and they were considering ways of assisting the expansion of industry. The government brought into effect with that budget what I feel is, by all standards of comparison, the best system of fiscal incentive to industry to undertake research that any country has today.
The present arrangements are that a research project approved by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) entitles the company to a deduction of current expenses without limit, that is to say up to 100 per cent of all profit can go into research and can be fully deducted. I do not see how that could be improved. A company can
